1.topic: Greed in the Bible: comparing Ahab and Gehazi, and its effects on society
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain the effects of Ahab's greed on Naboth, on justice in Israel and on Ahab's own house (1 Kings 21:1-29);
2. compare the greed of Ahab and of Gehazi (2 Kings 5:15-27);
3. relate the biblical teaching on greed to corruption and the love of money in society (Luke 12:13-21; 1 Timothy 6:6-10).

## Materials

Bibles, a comparison table on the board, short newspaper items on bribery and misuse of public funds.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: what is the difference between being rich and being greedy? Can a poor person be greedy? Take three answers.

## Development

1. Revise the two narratives briefly, using a table of cause, method and result for each.
2. Study the effect of Ahab's greed on three levels: a victim (Naboth), a community (the elders and false witnesses) and a family (Elijah's judgment).
3. Compare Ahab and Gehazi on the method used and the punishment suffered.
4. Read Luke 12:13-21, the parable of the rich fool, and 1 Timothy 6:6-10. Discuss "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil".
5. Apply to modern society: bribery, fraud, corruption and exam malpractice.

## Class activity

Students debate: "Greed is the root of corruption in Nigeria." Each side must use a verse.

## Evaluation

1. What does 1 Timothy 6:10 say about the love of money?
2. How did Gehazi try to hide what he had done?

## Assignment

Write an essay of about 250 words, "Greed in the Bible and in our society".

reading.title: The love of money and what it costs
reading.content:
# The love of money and what it costs

The Bible does not condemn wealth in itself, but it warns repeatedly against **greed**, the uncontrolled desire for more. Jesus told a crowd, "Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; life does not consist in an abundance of possessions" (Luke 12:15). He then told the parable of a rich farmer who stored up his harvest in bigger barns and planned to relax, but God said, "You fool! This very night your life will be demanded from you." Paul wrote, "People who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap... For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil" (1 Timothy 6:9-10).

## The effects of Ahab's greed (1 Kings 21)

1. **On Naboth.** An innocent man lost his life and his family's inheritance. Ahab and Jezebel used the law itself to destroy him, by hiring two false witnesses, using a fast day to disguise their plot and executing him on a charge of cursing God and the king.
2. **On the community.** The elders of Jezreel obeyed the royal letter and gave in to the king, instead of protecting justice. The courts were corrupted, and the poor man had no protection.
3. **On the king's house.** Elijah announced that Ahab's descendants would be cut off and that Jezebel would be eaten by dogs. Ahab's greed ruined his own family.

## Ahab and Gehazi compared

| | Ahab | Gehazi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What he wanted | Naboth's vineyard | Naaman's silver and clothes |
| Method | Used his wife and the royal seal, with false witnesses | Ran after Naaman with a lie about two prophets |
| Cover-up | Took possession and acted as if nothing had happened | Hid the silver; lied to Elisha |
| Position | A king using his power | A servant abusing his master's name |
| Result | Judgment announced, delayed because Ahab humbled himself | Immediate leprosy on him and his descendants |

**Similarities:** both coveted what belonged to another, both used deceit, both were confronted by a prophet and both suffered. **Differences:** the king acted through other people and the servant acted alone; Ahab's punishment was delayed after he repented, but Gehazi's came at once.

## Greed in society today

The same pattern appears today: public officials who take bribes, contractors who inflate bills, traders who give false weights, and students who pay for examination answers. The sufferers are often the weak, as Naboth was. A Christian should be content (1 Timothy 6:6-8), honest in all dealings, and ready to share.

2.topic: Josiah's reforms: why they could not save Judah, and lessons for leaders
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain why Josiah's reforms did not prevent the exile (2 Kings 22:14-20; 23:26-27);
2. describe what happened in Judah after Josiah's death (2 Kings 23:29-37);
3. draw lessons for religious and political leaders today.

## Materials

Bibles, a timeline of the kings of Judah from Hezekiah to Zedekiah, a chart of the reforms and their limits.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why do some reforms in a school or nation last, and others fade after the leader goes? Take answers and list reasons on the board.

## Development

1. Revise briefly the discovery of the Book of the Law and the reforms (2 Kings 22 to 23:25).
2. Read 2 Kings 22:14-20 and 23:26-27. Ask why God's anger did not turn away.
3. Read 2 Kings 23:29-37. Josiah's death at Megiddo, Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim.
4. Discuss the difference between enforced reform and a change of heart. Look at the people's response in 2 Kings 23:3.
5. Draw out the lessons for a modern leader, pastor or head of an institution.

## Class activity

Students write a short note "Advice to a new leader who wants to reform his organisation", citing Josiah.

## Evaluation

1. Why did God say the disaster would not come in Josiah's lifetime?
2. Who killed Josiah?

## Assignment

Write an essay of about 250 words on the strengths and limits of Josiah's reforms.

reading.title: Reform that came too late
reading.content:
# Reform that came too late

Josiah is remembered as the best of Judah's kings after David. When the Book of the Law was found, he led a thorough reform: the covenant was renewed, the temple was cleansed, the high places were destroyed and the Passover was kept. The writer says that "neither before nor after Josiah was there a king like him" (2 Kings 23:25). Yet the reforms did not save Judah. Why not?

## Why the reforms could not save Judah

1. **The sins of Manasseh.** The writer says that "the Lord did not turn away from the heat of his fierce anger, which burned against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke him" (23:26-27). Manasseh had ruled for fifty-five years, filled Jerusalem with idols, and shed much innocent blood. The damage was too deep to be undone by one reign.
2. **God's word through Huldah.** The prophetess had already told Josiah's officials that disaster would come on Judah because the people had forsaken God. Josiah's humility delayed it, but did not cancel it (22:16-20).
3. **The reform depended on the king.** The people joined the covenant, but the account shows that the change was led from above. After Josiah died, the next kings quickly returned to the old ways. Of Josiah's son Jehoahaz it is said that he "did evil in the eyes of the Lord", and the same is said of Jehoiakim (23:32, 37).
4. **Josiah's death.** In 609 BC Josiah went out to meet Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, who was marching to help Assyria, and was killed at Megiddo (23:29-30). The land came under the control of Egypt and then of Babylon.

## What happened afterwards

Pharaoh Necho took Jehoahaz to Egypt after only three months, and placed Jehoiakim on the throne, making Judah pay tribute. Within a generation, Babylon invaded, and the city and the temple were destroyed (2 Kings 24 and 25).

## Lessons

- **Reform must reach the heart.** Removing idols is not enough unless people truly turn to God.
- **A leader should raise others.** Josiah's reform ended with him because it was not rooted in a generation of followers.
- **Humility is rewarded.** Josiah's response to the word of God earned him a peaceful end and delayed the judgment.
- **The word of God is the basis of lasting renewal.** The reform began when the Book of the Law was found, read and obeyed.
- **Past wrongs have lasting results.** A nation cannot ignore the sins of the past.

3.topic: Concern for the nation: the fall of Jerusalem and the work of Nehemiah and Ezra
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe the condition of Judah leading up to the exile (2 Kings 24; 25:1-17);
2. outline how Nehemiah responded to the state of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1; 2:9-20; 4);

Bibles, a timeline from 605 BC to 430 BC, a map of Babylon, Susa and Jerusalem.

reading.title: Ruin and rebuilding
reading.content:
# Ruin and rebuilding

## The condition of the nation (2 Kings 24 and 25:1-17)

The last years of Judah were years of rebellion and defeat. King Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon for three years and then rebelled, and Babylon sent raiding bands against Judah (24:1-2). His son Jehoiachin surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC, and the king, the royal family, the officials and ten thousand of the best people, including craftsmen and metalworkers, were taken to Babylon. Only the poorest remained (24:10-16). The Babylonians appointed Zedekiah as king, but he rebelled too.

Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem for about two years until famine was severe in the city. In 586 BC the wall was breached. Zedekiah fled and was caught at Jericho. His sons were killed before his eyes, then he was blinded and taken in chains to Babylon. A month later, the commander Nebuzaradan burned the temple of the Lord, the palace and all the houses of Jerusalem, broke down the walls and carried off the bronze and gold furnishings of the temple. Most of the people were exiled (25:1-17). The writer shows that the disaster came because the people and their kings had turned from the Lord.

## The return and the response

**Ezra 1.** In 538 BC Cyrus of Persia issued a decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the temple. About fifty thousand returned under Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel. The work was opposed (Ezra 4), but after the prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the builders (5:1-2) the temple was completed and dedicated, and the Passover was celebrated with joy (6:13-22).

**Ezra the priest and scribe.** About 458 BC, Ezra came to Jerusalem with the king's blessing. The writer says, "Ezra had devoted himself to the study and observance of the Law of the Lord, and to teaching its decrees and laws in Israel" (Ezra 7:10).

**Nehemiah.** Nehemiah, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes at Susa, heard from his brother Hanani that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and its gates burned. He sat down and wept, mourned, fasted and prayed for days, confessing the sins of Israel (Nehemiah 1). When the king noticed his sad face, he asked for leave and for letters of safe passage and timber (2:1-8). Arriving in Jerusalem, he inspected the walls secretly at night and then challenged the leaders: "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem." They answered, "Let us start rebuilding." Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem mocked them, but Nehemiah replied, "The God of heaven will give us success" (2:9-20).

When the opposition became threatening, Nehemiah said, "We prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night" (4:9). Half the men worked and half held spears, shields and bows; the builders each wore a sword at the side. They finished the wall in fifty-two days.

## Lessons

Concern for the nation begins with prayer, continues with planning, and requires courage and teamwork.

4.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. narrate the story of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace (Daniel 3);
2. narrate the story of Daniel in the lions' den (Daniel 6);
3. state what the two stories teach about faith, courage and the power of God.

## Materials

Bibles, a picture of a furnace and of a lions' den, a chart "Faith and courage" and "Faith and power".

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: have you ever been pressured to do something you knew was wrong just because everyone else was doing it? How did you handle it?

## Development

1. Background: the exile in Babylon and the rise of Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1 and 2).
2. Read Daniel 3: the golden image, the decree, the refusal, the furnace and the fourth figure.
3. Read Daniel 6: the high office of Daniel, the jealous officials, the decree, the three daily prayers, the lions and Darius's decree.
4. Compare the two stories: pressure to compromise, firm obedience, deliverance, king's confession.
5. Draw out lessons on courage, consistency and trust in God.

## Class activity

Students list what each of the four men risked and what each gained.

## Evaluation

1. What was the reply of the three friends to Nebuchadnezzar?
2. How often did Daniel pray each day?

## Assignment

Write an essay of about 250 words: "Faith that stands under pressure".

# Faith that does not bow

## The fiery furnace (Daniel 3)

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon made a golden image, about ninety feet high, and set it up on the plain of Dura. He ordered all officials to bow down to it whenever the music played, on pain of being thrown into a blazing furnace. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, three Jewish officials, refused. Some astrologers reported them. The king was furious and gave them another chance. They answered him: "If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty's hand. But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up" (3:17-18).

The king ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter, and the three men were bound and thrown in. The flames killed the soldiers who threw them. But the king, watching, was amazed: "Look! I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods." The three were called out, and not even a hair of their heads was singed, and they did not smell of fire. Nebuchadnezzar praised their God and decreed that no one should speak against Him.

**Lesson (faith and courage):** their faith did not depend on the outcome. They obeyed God even if He did not rescue them.

## The lions' den (Daniel 6)

Under King Darius the Mede, Daniel was so capable that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. Jealous officials looked for a charge against him but found none, because he was trustworthy. They persuaded the king to sign a decree that for thirty days anyone who prayed to any god or man except the king would be thrown into the lions' den. Daniel heard of the decree but went to his upstairs room, where the windows opened towards Jerusalem, and prayed three times a day, giving thanks to God, just as he had always done.

The officials reported him. Darius, who was distressed, tried to save him until sunset, but the law could not be changed. Daniel was thrown to the lions, and the king said, "May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you." The den was sealed. The king passed a sleepless night, and at dawn hurried to the den. Daniel answered, "My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight." Daniel was lifted out unharmed "because he had trusted in his God". The men who had accused him were thrown into the den. Darius decreed that people in every part of his kingdom should fear and reverence the God of Daniel.

**Lesson (faith and power):** God has power over kings, laws and wild animals; He protects those who trust Him.

## What the stories teach

- Obey God before human commands that contradict His.
- Be consistent in faith whether or not it is safe.
- God's presence is with His people in trials.
- Faithful witness can lead rulers to acknowledge God.

reading.content:
# A God of justice and a God of love

## Amos: true religion and social justice

Amos was a shepherd and farmer from Tekoa in Judah, called by God to prophesy in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II (about 760 BC). It was a time of prosperity and military success, but the wealth was in the hands of a few, and the poor were oppressed.

**What Amos condemned**

- The rich sold "the innocent for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals". They trampled on the heads of the poor and denied justice to the oppressed (2:6-7).
- Merchants cheated: they could not wait for the festival to end so they could sell grain, and they made the ephah small and the shekel large and cheated with dishonest scales (8:4-6).
- Wealthy women, whom he called "cows of Bashan", oppressed the poor and demanded drinks from their husbands (4:1).
- People worshipped at Bethel and Gilgal but their religion was a show (4:4-5).

Through Amos, God said, "I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me... But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!" (5:21, 24). God cares more about right living than ritual.

When Amos prophesied that Jeroboam would die by the sword, Amaziah the priest of Bethel told him to go home to Judah and not prophesy there. Amos replied that he was no professional prophet, but a shepherd whom the Lord had called (7:10-15).

**Nature of God taught by Amos:** God is just, He hates oppression, He requires righteousness, and He judges nations and His own people for sin.

## Hosea: God's faithful love

Hosea prophesied in Israel a little later. God told him to marry Gomer, a woman who would be unfaithful to him. Their children were given symbolic names: Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah ("not loved") and Lo-Ammi ("not my people") (Hosea 1). Gomer left Hosea for other lovers. The marriage pictured God's relationship with Israel, who had gone after Baal and other gods. God said Israel's guilt would bring punishment (Hosea 2), yet He would win her back.

In chapter 3 God told Hosea to love his wife again, though she had gone to another man. Hosea bought her back for fifteen shekels of silver and some barley. This pictured God's redemption of Israel.

In Hosea 6:6 God declares, "For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings."

**Nature of God taught by Hosea:** God is loving and faithful even when His people are unfaithful. He is jealous for His people's loyalty, He disciplines, and He forgives those who return.

## Lessons

- True religion shows itself in justice, honesty and mercy.
- God loves His people with a faithful love and calls them to return.
- Ritual without right living is rejected by God.

6.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. compare the accounts of the baptism of Jesus in Matthew, Mark and Luke (Matthew 3:13-17; Mark 1:9-11; Luke 3:21-22);
2. compare the accounts of the temptation of Jesus (Matthew 4:1-11; Mark 1:12-13; Luke 4:1-13);
3. explain the significance of the baptism and the temptation for Christians.

## Materials

Bibles, a three-column chart headed Matthew, Mark and Luke, markers.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why do three people who saw the same event often tell it a little differently? Link this to the Synoptic Gospels, which "see together".

## Development

1. Define "Synoptic": Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material and a similar outline.
2. Read the three accounts of the baptism side by side. Complete the chart: who spoke, what was said, what was seen, where Jesus prayed.
3. Read the three accounts of the temptation. Note that Mark is very short, while Matthew and Luke give three temptations in different order.
4. Discuss the answer of Jesus each time: Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13.
5. Discuss the significance for Christians: identification, the Spirit, sonship, victory over temptation.

## Class activity

Students complete the chart, then state in two sentences one similarity and one difference between the accounts.

## Evaluation

1. What does Luke add about the baptism of Jesus?
2. In what order does Luke place the temptations?

## Assignment

Write about 250 words on what Christians learn from the temptation of Jesus.

reading.title: Three witnesses, one story
reading.content:
# Three witnesses, one story

The first three Gospels are called the **Synoptic Gospels**. They share a similar outline, and often similar words. Reading them side by side helps us see both their agreement and the special emphasis of each writer.

## The baptism of Jesus

All three agree that Jesus was baptised by John in the Jordan, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended on Him like a dove, and a voice from heaven spoke.

- **Matthew 3:13-17.** Only Matthew records the conversation in which John tried to stop Jesus ("I need to be baptised by you"), and Jesus' answer, "It is proper for us to do this to fulfil all righteousness." The voice speaks about Jesus: "This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased."
- **Mark 1:9-11.** The shortest account. The voice speaks directly to Jesus: "You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased." Mark records that Jesus saw heaven being "torn open".
- **Luke 3:21-22.** Luke mentions that Jesus was praying when the heavens opened, and that the Spirit descended "in bodily form like a dove". The voice also speaks to Jesus.

**Significance:** Jesus identified Himself with sinful humanity and began His public work. He was anointed by the Spirit for ministry and affirmed as the beloved Son of God. Christian baptism follows His example.

## The temptation of Jesus

After His baptism the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness. All three Gospels say that He was tempted by the devil.

- **Mark 1:12-13** gives only two verses: Jesus was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan, was with wild animals, and angels attended Him.
- **Matthew 4:1-11** gives the three temptations in this order: turn stones to bread; throw yourself from the temple pinnacle; worship the devil to gain all the kingdoms. Jesus answered from Deuteronomy each time. Then the devil left and angels attended Him.
- **Luke 4:1-13** gives the same three, but in a different order: stones to bread, the kingdoms, and then the temple, ending in Jerusalem. Luke adds that the devil left Him "until an opportune time".

**The temptations tested Jesus' trust in His Father:** to use His power to satisfy His own needs, to prove Himself by a spectacular sign, and to gain power without the cross.

**Significance:** Jesus is able to help those who are tempted, because He was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His use of Scripture is an example: we resist temptation by knowing and obeying God's word.

8.topic: The call and demands of discipleship
8.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. narrate the call of the first disciples and of Levi (Matthew 4:18-25; 9:9-13; Mark 1:16-20; 2:13-17; Luke 5:1-11);
2. state the demands of discipleship (Matthew 8:18-22; Luke 9:57-62; 14:25-33);
3. apply the demands of discipleship to the life of a Christian student.

## Materials

Bibles, a chart of the calls recorded in the Synoptic Gospels, cards for a "count the cost" discussion.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: what are the qualities of a good student in this school? What would a student have to give up to be the best in the class? Link it to the cost of following Jesus.

## Development

1. Define a disciple: a learner and follower. Read Mark 1:16-20, Luke 5:1-11 and Matthew 4:18-25 for the call of the fishermen.
2. Read Matthew 9:9-13 and Mark 2:13-17: the call of Levi and the meal.
3. Read Matthew 8:18-22 and Luke 9:57-62: three would-be followers and Jesus' replies.
4. Read Luke 14:25-33: putting Jesus first, carrying the cross, counting the cost.
5. Discuss which demands are hardest today.

## Class activity

Groups write a "job description" for a disciple using the demands in Luke 14.

## Evaluation

1. What did Peter say when he saw the great catch of fish?
2. What two pictures did Jesus use about counting the cost?

reading.title: Follow me, and count the cost
reading.content:
# Follow me, and count the cost

A **disciple** is a learner and follower. In the Gospels, Jesus called ordinary people to follow Him, and He made clear that following Him meant a changed life.

## The call of the first disciples

At the lake of Galilee Jesus called Simon and Andrew, then James and John, who were fishermen. Luke adds that Jesus first taught the crowd from Simon's boat, then told him to put out into deep water and let down the nets. Simon said they had fished all night and caught nothing, "but because you say so, I will let down the nets." They caught so many fish that their nets began to break. Simon fell at Jesus' knees and said, "Go away from me, Lord; I am a sinful man!" Jesus replied, "Don't be afraid; from now on you will fish for people." They pulled their boats up on shore, left everything and followed Him (Luke 5:1-11; Mark 1:16-20).

## The call of Levi (Matthew)

Jesus saw a tax collector named Levi (Matthew) sitting at his tax booth and said, "Follow me." Levi got up, left everything and followed Him. Then he gave a great banquet in his house with many tax collectors and sinners. The Pharisees complained. Jesus answered, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick... I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners" (Matthew 9:9-13; Mark 2:13-17; Luke 5:27-32). Tax collectors were hated as collaborators with Rome and as cheats. Jesus' call was open to everyone.

## Three would-be followers (Luke 9:57-62; Matthew 8:18-22)

1. One said, "I will follow you wherever you go." Jesus replied, "Foxes have dens and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head." Discipleship may mean giving up comfort and security.
2. Another asked to bury his father first. Jesus said, "Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God." The kingdom comes first.
3. Another wanted to say farewell to his family. Jesus said, "No one who puts a hand to the plough and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God." Discipleship needs total commitment.

## The cost of being a disciple (Luke 14:25-33)

Great crowds followed Jesus, and He turned and said that anyone who comes to Him must "hate" his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, even his own life. "Hate" here is a strong way of saying that loyalty to Jesus must come before every other loyalty. A disciple must carry his own cross, which means being ready to suffer and to die to self. Jesus used two pictures. A man who wants to build a tower first sits down and estimates the cost, or he will be laughed at. A king going to war first considers whether his ten thousand men can face twenty thousand. In the same way, "those of you who do not give up everything you have cannot be my disciples."

## Summary of the demands

- Put Jesus first, before family and possessions.
- Be ready to give up comfort and security.
- Follow without delay and without looking back.
- Carry the cross daily.
- Count the cost before beginning.

reading.title: Forgiven, therefore forgiving
reading.content:
# Forgiven, therefore forgiving

## Forgiveness in the Lord's Prayer

In the Lord's Prayer, Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). He then added: "For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins" (6:14-15). Forgiveness from God and forgiveness from us are linked. A person who refuses to forgive shows that he has not understood how much he has been forgiven.

## Peter's question (Matthew 18:21-22)

Peter asked Jesus, "Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother or sister who sins against me? Up to seven times?" The Jewish teachers taught that three times was enough, so Peter thought he was being generous. Jesus replied, "I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times." The number means that there is no limit to forgiveness.

## The parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:23-35)

A king decided to settle accounts with his servants. One servant was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents, a sum so enormous that he could never repay it. The king ordered that he, his wife, his children and all he owned be sold to pay the debt. The servant fell on his knees and begged, "Be patient with me, and I will pay back everything." The king took pity on him, cancelled the debt and let him go.

That servant went out and found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, a small sum, the wage of a hundred days. He grabbed him by the throat and demanded, "Pay back what you owe me!" The fellow servant begged for patience in the same words, but the first refused and had him thrown into prison.

The other servants were distressed and reported it to the king. The king summoned the servant: "You wicked servant, I cancelled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?" In anger the king handed him over to the jailers to be tortured until he should pay back all he owed. 10.topic: The trials of Jesus: Gethsemane, Peter's denials and the arrest
10.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. narrate the prayer of Jesus in Gethsemane and His arrest (Matthew 26:36-56; Mark 14:32-52);
2. narrate Peter's three denials (Matthew 26:69-75; Mark 14:66-72; Luke 22:54-62);
3. summarise the condemnation of Jesus by the Sanhedrin (Matthew 26:57-68; Mark 14:53-65; Luke 22:66-71) and Jesus before Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:1-12);
4. draw lessons from these events.

## Materials

Bibles, a map of Jerusalem showing the Mount of Olives, the high priest's house and Pilate's headquarters.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: what would you do if you knew something painful was about to happen, and you had the chance to avoid it? Link the answers to Jesus in the garden.

## Development

1. Read Matthew 26:36-46. Note who Jesus took with Him, what He prayed, and the disciples' sleep.
2. Read Matthew 26:47-56. Judas's kiss, Peter's sword, Jesus' rebuke and the flight of the disciples.
3. Read Luke 22:54-62. The three denials and the look of Jesus.
4. Summarise the trial before the Sanhedrin and the verdict (Mark 14:53-65), then Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:1-12).
5. Draw lessons on prayer, loyalty, failure and forgiveness.

## Class activity

Students make a timeline of the night from the Last Supper to the morning.

## Evaluation

1. Which three disciples did Jesus take further into the garden?
2. What happened when the cock crowed?

## Assignment

Write about 250 words on what the trials of Jesus teach about courage.

reading.content:
# The longest night

## Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36-46; Mark 14:32-42)

After the Last Supper, Jesus took His disciples to a place called Gethsemane, on the Mount of Olives. He told eight of them to sit while He prayed, and took Peter, James and John further. He said, "My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with me." Going a little further, He fell with His face to the ground and prayed, "My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will" (Matthew 26:39). The cup stands for the suffering He was about to face.

Three times He returned and found the disciples asleep. He said to Peter, "Couldn't you men keep watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak."

## The arrest (Matthew 26:47-56)

While Jesus was still speaking, Judas arrived with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs sent by the chief priests and elders. Judas had given them a sign: "The one I kiss is the man; arrest him." He went up to Jesus and said, "Greetings, Rabbi!" and kissed Him. Jesus replied, "Do what you came for, friend." One of the disciples (John says it was Peter) drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus told him, "Put your sword back in its place, for all who draw the sword will die by the sword." He said He could call twelve legions of angels, but the Scriptures had to be fulfilled. Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.

## Peter's denials (Luke 22:54-62; Matthew 26:69-75)

Jesus was led to the high priest's house. Peter followed at a distance and sat by a fire in the courtyard. A servant girl said, "This man was with him." Peter denied it. A little later someone said, "You also are one of them." Peter denied again, with an oath. About an hour later, bystanders said, "Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away." Peter began to curse and swear, "I don't know the man!" Just then the cock crowed. The Lord turned and looked straight at Peter. Peter remembered Jesus' words, "Before the cock crows today, you will disown me three times," and he went outside and wept bitterly.

## The condemnation

Before the Sanhedrin, false witnesses were brought, but their stories did not agree. The high priest Caiaphas asked, "Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus said, "I am," and added that they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Mighty One. Caiaphas tore his clothes and charged Him with blasphemy, and the council condemned Him as worthy of death (Mark 14:53-65). In the morning Jesus was taken to Pilate, accused of misleading the nation, then sent to Herod Antipas, who mocked Him and sent Him back (Luke 23:1-12).

## Lessons

- Pray in times of trial and submit to the Father's will.
- Be watchful; good intentions are not enough without strength.
- Failure can be forgiven; Peter wept and was later restored.
- Jesus accepted the cross willingly and not as a helpless victim.
